newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors deny decision on Iran probe.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors deny decision on Iran probe.

text.p: German prosecutors on Wednesday denied they had decided to launch a criminal probe of Iran's foreign minister, saying they were still considering whether to investigate Iranian officials "at all levels".

A spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office said it was studying last week's verdict by a German court that top Iranian leaders ordered the 1992 killing of four dissidents in Berlin. But she said the office had not yet come to a decision.
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper had said the prosecutor's office had decided formally to launch investigations into Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati.
"That's not true," the spokeswoman said, stressing the question was still open.
She said officials were checking whether there were grounds for investigation against Iranian suspects "at all levels". A decision was unlikely to be reached this week, she said.
She said the checks would include deciding whether some suspects were immune on political or diplomatic grounds.
The newspaper said prosecutors had ruled out proceedings against Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and religious leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei because of "immunity problems".

The Frankfurter Allgemeine also reported investigators had searched the offices of a company in the Frankfurt area earlier this month as part of a probe into allegations of illegal arms procurement by Iran.
Prosecutors confirmed an investigation was under way but declined to comment on any details. Opposition politicians, however, were quick to condemn Iran.
"The court in Berlin has scarcely announced its verdict and already further criminal activities are appearing," the opposition Social Democrats said.

The issue looked set to remain controversial as parliament announced it would hold a debate on relations with Iran on Thursday. The opposition Greens party submitted a motion calling for diplomatic ties to be "frozen at a minimum".
Iranians have staged several marches on German's Tehran embassy and, according to Tehran radio, protested in two dozen cities across the country in the wake of last week's court verdict.

It was the first time a European court had clearly attributed political responsibility for any of the dozens of assassinations of Iranian opposition figures abroad since the Islamic revolution in 1979.

The court said Iranian leaders including the state president and the religious leader had ordered the killings. But it only mentioned Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan by name. Iran has denied any involvement.
